newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION-In defence of S.Africa's Stals-By M.Bester.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-In defence of S.Africa's Stals-By M.Bester.

text.p: By Michiel Bester, economist at Econometrix (Pty) Ltd
In recent weeks criticism of Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals has arisen from business, the unions, economists and academics.
These critics have all argued that the Bank rate should be reduced.
At the same time there was a discussion around the possible amendment of the Reserve Bank Act to bring about a greater transparency of monetary policy formulation.

One proposal is that monetary policy should be determined by a committee with Reserve Bank staff, as well as members appointed by government. This proposal could also be seen as implicit criticism of the policy approach of Stals.
Against this background it is important to state the benefits of the policies of Stals. He has been governor of the South African Reserve Bank since August 1989.
The policies of Stals played a major role in reducing inflation. It is not the only factor, but an important one.
In the three years before he became governor consumer price inflation averaged 14.9 percent. For the last three years the corresponding figure is 8.5 percent.
The benefits of lower inflation are many, but three can be emphasised.

First, lower inflation, relative to that of trading partners, necessitates less rand depreciation, which contributes to lower domestic inflation. The replacement of a vicious circle with a virtuous one has to start somewhere. Stals lead the way.
Second, lower inflation makes planning for the future easier. This contributes to higher fixed investment.
Third, inflation affects the poor, usually wage earners and pensioners, more adversely than higher income groups.

Monetary policy should create a stable monetary and financial environment so that growth in the real sector can flourish, inter alia, because planning for the future becomes easier and facilitates higher growth in fixed investment.
This is the point of departure of Stals. The contribution of monetary policy to higher growth is therefore mainly an indirect one.
His critics may not accept this premise, or seem unwilling to recognise that this is Stals' point of departure. He does not simply focus on inflation. His focus is a wider one.
Since Stals has been governor, the volatility of interest rates and rand depreciation has been much less than during most of the eighties.
Stals wants to avoid the stop-go policies which characterised much of the seventies and eighties.

Stals has over the years in his annual governor's addresses and speeches clearly spelt out the criteria which the central bank considers when taking decisions on the appropriate level of the Bank rate.
In the short-term there are four criteria -- inflation, money and credit growth, the balance of payments or the rand and trading partner interest rates.
Other factors may be considered in the longer-term, such as savings rate or the prudence of fiscal policies.

Thus it may be argued that present inflation and the balance of payments are at acceptable levels for a cut in the Bank rate, but that the growth of money and especially of credit to the private sector is too high.
The latter does, in part, reflect inflationary expectations.
It is probable that the high growth of private credit is due to structural factors, but until this is well established, it would be unwise to cut the Bank rate.
South African real short-term rates are higher than in its major trading partners and thus are not out of line with trading partner interest rates.
Consistency of policy raises the level of certainty which is good for fixed investment in the long-term.

High interest rates, in nominal and real terms undoubtedly contribute to lower growth, but there are other factors too. It is simply not true to state that high rates are undermining government's Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy.
First, the decline in gold mining output is one cause of slower growth. Second, fiscal policy has become restrictive.
Third, the spurt in private fixed investment in new machinery in equipment, which started in 1994, has lost some momentum, which is to some extent natural and not simply due to high interest rates.

Fourth, consumers have become very indebted and have difficulty in servicing their debt. This difficulty is not simply due to higher interest rates, but also to high debt levels, which is the result of the high growth in their borrowing of the past two years.

Fifth, the growth in infrastructural investment is hindered by delays of an administrative and policy formulation nature. It should also be remembered that the positive factors mentioned above, have made a contribution to the inflows of foreign direct and portfolio investments and have increased the availability of short-term foreign loans to finance the current account deficit.
This is a major positive contribution.
The criticism of Stals generally does not recognise the major positive contributions which he has made to economic policy.
There is also a tendency to emphasise single issues and short-term considerations.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
